name: Canada
tagline: Turquoise glacial lakes, French colonial old towns and a thundering waterfall shared with the United States, spread across the world's second-largest country.
cardDescription: The Rockies' turquoise lakes, Vancouver's mountains-to-sea setting, Old Quebec's French colonial streets, and Niagara Falls thundering over the border.
metaDescription: A complete Canada travel guide: the 10 best places to visit, getting around, food, costs, etiquette and a twelve-day Western Canada itinerary.

image.alt: Lake Louise's turquoise water in Banff National Park

intro: Canada is the world's second-largest country, and it shows — a first trip realistically means choosing one region rather than attempting anything resembling a full tour.

Its genuine range runs from the turquoise glacial lakes and jagged peaks of the Rockies to French colonial old towns in Quebec, from a waterfall shared with the United States to a remote Hudson Bay outpost known as the polar bear capital of the world.

What ties it together is a strong regional identity — Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal and Quebec City each feel like a different country's capital, and the trip you plan should lean into that rather than fight it.
placesIntro: Ordered roughly by how strongly we would recommend each for a first visit — though Canada's sheer scale means the right answer depends heavily on which region you're drawn to.
thingsToDoIntro: The experiences that recur across the country and make a Canada trip feel like more than a checklist of cities.

thingsToDo.title: Canoe a turquoise glacial lake

image.alt: A turquoise glacial lake in the Canadian Rockies

thingsToDo.text: An essential Rockies experience, paddling water coloured an almost unbelievable turquoise by glacial rock flour.
thingsToDo.tip: Arrive at opening time at the most famous lakes — parking and crowds both build fast by mid-morning.

thingsToDo.title: Drive the Icefields Parkway

image.file: File:Icefields Parkway from an elevated viewpoint, Jasper National Park, Alberta, Canada.jpg
image.alt: The Icefields Parkway between Banff and Jasper

thingsToDo.text: A spectacular drive, glaciers, waterfalls and jagged peaks lining the road between Banff and Jasper.
thingsToDo.tip: Budget a full day for the drive alone, with stops — rushing it defeats the point.

thingsToDo.title: Eat poutine

image.alt: Poutine, Canada's fries, cheese curds and gravy dish

thingsToDo.text: An essential Canadian dish, fries topped with cheese curds and gravy, found everywhere from diners to food trucks.
thingsToDo.tip: Seek out a Quebec version for the most authentic take on the dish's home province.

thingsToDo.title: Watch for moose and bears in the wild

image.alt: A moose in the Canadian wilderness

thingsToDo.text: A thrilling, if unpredictable, part of Rockies travel, spotting wildlife along roadsides and trails.
thingsToDo.tip: Never approach for a photo — view from a vehicle or at a safe, respectful distance.

thingsToDo.title: Wander Old Quebec's colonial streets
thingsToDo.text: A singular experience in North America, the continent's only walled city north of Mexico.
thingsToDo.tip: Visit in the early morning before day-trippers arrive from cruise ships and tour buses.

thingsToDo.title: Visit a sugar shack in maple season

image.alt: A traditional Canadian maple sugar shack

thingsToDo.text: A lovely spring ritual in Quebec and Ontario, tasting fresh maple syrup straight from the source.
thingsToDo.tip: Time a visit for late winter into early spring, when sap is actually running.

foodIntro: Canadian food varies sharply by region, from Quebec's distinct table to Maritime seafood and Prairie beef.

foods.name: Poutine

image.alt: Poutine, Canada's fries, cheese curds and gravy dish

foods.text: Canada's best-known dish, fries topped with cheese curds and gravy, born in rural Quebec.
foods.whereToTry: Found nationwide, though Quebec is the place to try it properly.

foods.name: Montreal-style bagels
foods.text: Distinct from New York bagels, smaller, sweeter and wood-fired, a real point of local pride.
foods.whereToTry: Bagel bakeries throughout Montreal, especially the city's oldest ones.

foods.name: Nanaimo bars

image.alt: A Nanaimo bar, a layered Canadian dessert

foods.text: A no-bake layered dessert named for the British Columbia town where it originated.
foods.whereToTry: Bakeries and cafés throughout British Columbia and beyond.

foods.name: Maple syrup

image.alt: Maple sap collection, the start of Canadian maple syrup production

foods.text: One of the country's defining exports, Quebec alone producing most of the world's supply.
foods.whereToTry: Sugar shacks and markets throughout Quebec and Ontario.

foods.name: Butter tarts

image.file: File:Butter tarts it's a Canadian thing. (47104703864).jpg
image.alt: Butter tarts, a classic Canadian pastry

foods.text: A beloved, distinctly Canadian pastry, a flaky shell filled with a sweet, gooey butter and sugar filling.

foods.name: Maritime lobster
foods.text: A real highlight of the East Coast, fresh lobster served simply, often straight from the boat.
foods.whereToTry: Seafood shacks throughout Prince Edward Island and the wider Maritimes.

practicalIntro: The essentials for planning a Canada trip, gathered in one place.

practical.language: English and French, Canada's two official languages; French predominates in Quebec.
practical.money: Card-friendly everywhere, including tap-to-pay for small purchases; cash is rarely needed.
practical.visa: Visa-exempt travellers arriving by air need an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA); US citizens need only a valid passport. Visa-free stays run up to six months for most eligible nationalities.
practical.plugs: Type A and B, 120 V, 60 Hz — the same as the United States.
practical.tipping: Expected, American-style — 15–20% at restaurants, similar for taxis and personal services.
practical.safety: One of the world's safer countries, with normal city precautions being all that's typically needed.
practical.connectivity: Excellent in cities, noticeably patchier and pricier in remote northern regions like Churchill.
practical.timeZone: Spans six time zones, from Newfoundland (UTC-3:30) to Pacific (UTC-8); most regions observe daylight saving time.

budget.label: Backpacker
budget.value: C$90–140 per day — hostels, transit, casual meals

budget.label: Mid-range
budget.value: C$200–350 per day — 3-star hotels, restaurant dinners, some tours

budget.label: Comfortable
budget.value: C$400–700 per day — boutique hotels, guided park tours, car rental

budget.label: Rockies national park pass
budget.value: Add C$10–20 per person per day for Banff or Jasper entry

bestTime.headline: June to September for warm weather and open mountain roads
bestTime.summary: Canada's huge range means the best season depends heavily on region, though summer works well almost everywhere.

seasons.text: The most reliable season nationwide, with warm weather and every mountain road and trail open.
Excellent in the Rockies especially, with fall colour and noticeably thinner crowds than summer.
Superb for skiing in Whistler and Banff, and for aurora viewing further north, though many mountain roads and trails close.
A shoulder season with unpredictable weather, though still worthwhile in the cities.

bestTime.avoid: Nothing nationwide, though mountain hiking trails can stay snow-covered into June or July at higher elevations.

tripDuration.headline: 10–14 days for one region
tripDuration.summary: Canada is too large for a single trip to cover meaningfully — the real question is which region, not how long for 'Canada' as a whole.

options.text: One city, done properly, with an easy nearby addition. Vancouver pairs with Whistler; Toronto with Niagara Falls; Montreal with Quebec City.
options.detail: A good first Canada trip, and far better than a rushed multi-region one.

options.text: One region in full. Western Canada's Rockies loop (Vancouver, Whistler, Banff and Lake Louise, Jasper), or Eastern Canada's cities (Toronto, Niagara Falls, Montreal, Quebec City).
options.detail: The sweet spot for a first visit, and where a rental car earns its cost.

options.text: Two adjacent regions, or one region plus a distinctive add-on like Prince Edward Island or Churchill.
options.detail: At least one internal flight is needed — Canada's regions don't connect by a quick drive.

options.text: A genuine east-to-west route, though this means real time spent travelling given the distances involved.
options.detail: Via Rail's transcontinental train is a slower, scenic alternative to flying between regions.

transport.intro: Canada's vast distances mean flying between regions and driving within them, rather than any single mode covering everything.

options.text: Essential for connecting [[vancouver|Vancouver]] to [[toronto|Toronto]] or [[montreal|Montreal]], or reaching [[churchill|Churchill]].
options.detail: The distances involved are continental in scale — Vancouver to Toronto is a 4.5-hour flight.

options.text: The way to see [[banff-lake-louise|Banff and Lake Louise]], [[jasper-national-park|Jasper]] and [[prince-edward-island|Prince Edward Island]].
options.detail: Essential for reaching trailheads and viewpoints on your own schedule.

options.text: A scenic, slower alternative to flying, especially [[toronto|Toronto]] to [[vancouver|Vancouver]] via The Canadian.
options.detail: A multi-day journey best treated as part of the experience, not just transport.
Subway, streetcar and bus networks cover each downtown core well.

options.text: Useful for reaching [[niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]] from [[toronto|Toronto]], or [[whistler|Whistler]] from Vancouver.
options.detail: A car-free option for popular day trips and short hops.

itinerary.title: Twelve days in Western Canada
itinerary.intro: Canada is too large for a cross-country tour, so this covers one region properly: the classic Western Canada loop from Vancouver through the Coast Mountains to the Rockies. It is a driving route, and the driving is much of the point.

days.title: Arrive in Vancouver
days.morning: Land in Vancouver and check in to your hotel.
days.afternoon: Explore Gastown and the downtown waterfront.

days.title: Vancouver
days.morning: Stanley Park's seawall by bike or on foot.

days.title: The Sea to Sky Highway to Whistler
days.morning: Drive north along the Sea to Sky Highway.
days.afternoon: Stop at Shannon Falls and the Sea to Sky Gondola.
days.evening: Arrive in Whistler Village for dinner.

days.title: Whistler
days.morning: Ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola between Whistler and Blackcomb.
days.afternoon: Explore Whistler Village and Lost Lake.

days.title: Fly to Calgary and drive to Banff
days.morning: Return to Vancouver and fly to Calgary.
days.afternoon: Drive from Calgary into Banff National Park.

days.title: Banff town
days.morning: The Banff Gondola up Sulphur Mountain.
days.afternoon: Explore Banff Avenue and the Bow Falls trail.

days.title: Lake Louise and Moraine Lake
days.morning: Canoe or walk the shoreline at Lake Louise.
days.afternoon: Continue to Moraine Lake, if the access road is open.
days.evening: Return to Banff for a final night.

days.title: The Icefields Parkway to Jasper
days.morning: Depart Banff on the Icefields Parkway.
days.afternoon: Stop at the Athabasca Glacier and Sunwapta Falls.

days.title: Jasper National Park
days.morning: Boat trip on Maligne Lake to Spirit Island.
days.afternoon: Wildlife spotting along the Maligne Valley.

days.title: The Jasper SkyTram
days.morning: Ride the Jasper SkyTram for a mountain panorama.
days.afternoon: Explore Pyramid Lake or Patricia Lake.

days.title: Return to Calgary
days.morning: Drive back down the Icefields Parkway.
days.afternoon: Continue to Calgary, stopping in Banff if time allows.

days.title: Depart
days.morning: A final wander or last-minute shopping.

culture.intro: Canadian culture prizes politeness and multiculturalism as real, lived values, alongside a strong regional identity that varies sharply from coast to coast.

etiquette.title: Politeness is a real social norm
etiquette.text: Saying sorry, please and thank you liberally is standard, not performative.

etiquette.title: Tipping is expected, American-style
etiquette.text: 15–20% at restaurants; many card machines now prompt for it directly.

etiquette.title: Quebec's French identity is worth respecting
etiquette.text: Attempt a French greeting in Quebec — it's appreciated even if your French is limited.

etiquette.title: Queuing is taken seriously
etiquette.text: Lines are orderly, and cutting one is a real social faux pas.

etiquette.title: Indigenous land acknowledgements are common
etiquette.text: Many public events open by acknowledging the traditional First Nations territory.

etiquette.title: Personal space is valued
etiquette.text: Standing a comfortable arm's length away in conversation is the norm.

dos: Layer clothing for dramatic swings between regions and seasons.
Book national park passes ahead for Banff and Jasper in peak summer.
Try regional specialities — Quebec's food culture is distinct from the rest of the country.
Carry a light rain jacket in Vancouver and coastal British Columbia, even in summer.
donts: Don't assume one region represents the whole country — Canada's regions differ enormously.
Don't underestimate driving distances — 'nearby' on a Canadian map can still mean hours.
Don't approach wildlife in the Rockies, however calm it looks — moose and bears are dangerous.
Don't skip travel insurance — healthcare for visitors isn't covered by Canada's public system.

tipsIntro: Practical notes that make travel through Canada noticeably smoother.
tips: Book national park passes and popular lodges in Banff and Jasper well ahead for summer.
Pack for layered weather, even in summer — mountain evenings turn cold fast.
Rent a car for the Rockies — public transport doesn't reach most trailheads.
Carry bear spray and know how to use it before any backcountry hiking.
Consider Via Rail's scenic trains as a slower alternative to flying between regions.
Budget extra for national park entry fees, which add up on a multi-park trip.
Learn a few basic French phrases for Quebec and Montreal.
Check seasonal road closures before planning a Rockies itinerary outside summer.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Canada?
faq.a: Ten to fourteen days covers one region properly, such as the Western Canada Rockies loop in this guide's itinerary; a week suits a single city plus one nearby addition.
Comparable to the United States overall, with national park fees and Rockies lodging adding up on a mountain-focused trip.

faq.q: Do you need a car in Canada?
faq.a: Not for the major cities, which have good transit, but yes for the Rockies and Prince Edward Island.

faq.q: What language is spoken in Canada?
faq.a: English nationwide, with French as Quebec's primary language and Canada's other official language.
Yes — one of the world's safer countries, with typical city precautions being all that's usually needed.

faq.q: When can you see the northern lights in Canada?
faq.a: September through April in northern regions like Churchill, with the darkest winter months offering the best odds.
